exam_guide_revision: Reviewed anti-boring v4, 2026-09-26. Full learning and question editorial audit completed; weak/generic prompts and distractors were rewritten while preserving compatibility.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

glossary.definition: Discovered graph vertices waiting to be processed.
A set of vertices connected to one another under the graph's connectivity rule.
An ordering of a DAG where every prerequisite appears before each dependent vertex.
Trying an edge to see whether it improves the best known path cost to its destination.
The best path cost to a vertex known so far, before finalization.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

modules.title: Traverse relationships with the right frontier

nodes.title: When relationships stop looking like a tree, model the connections directly

reveal.text: A service can call several downstream services, and one downstream service can be shared by many callers. You are learning to recognize graph structure and track discovery so shared paths/cycles do not create repeated traversal.

spans.text: A service can call several downstream services, and one downstream service can be shared by many callers.

reveal.text: Forcing this into a strict tree duplicates shared services and hides cycles.

spans.text: many-to-many relationships do not fit one-parent hierarchy assumptions

reveal.text: Model services as vertices and calls as directed edges. During traversal, mark discovered vertices so alternate paths do not repeatedly re-add them.

nodes.title: Fewest hops? Let the frontier move in layers

reveal.text: Every service-to-service call counts as one hop. Find the minimum number of hops from gateway to database service. You are learning to use BFS when every edge has equal cost and the objective is minimum edge count.

spans.text: Every service-to-service call counts as one hop. Find the minimum number of hops from gateway to database service.
You are learning to use BFS when every edge has equal cost and the objective is minimum edge count

reveal.text: DFS may find a valid path quickly, but the first path it finds can be much longer than another unexplored path.

spans.text: depth-first discovery order does not guarantee minimum hop count

reveal.text: A FIFO queue processes all vertices at distance d before distance d+1. The first discovery gives a shortest hop count.

spans.text: FIFO frontier + discovered distance

reveal.text: BFS shortest path in unweighted graph. Trigger: fewest moves/hops/edges where every transition has equal cost

spans.text: BFS shortest path in unweighted graph
fewest moves/hops/edges where every transition has equal cost

reveal.text: Minimum delegation steps, minimum state transitions, and shortest maze moves all share the equal-cost frontier.

spans.text: layered FIFO expansion matches edge-count distance

reveal.text: If edge latencies differ, does BFS still minimize latency? Answer: No — it minimizes hop count, not weighted cost.

spans.text: No — it minimizes hop count, not weighted cost.

nodes.title: To detect a directed cycle, 'visited' is not enough — you need 'still active'

reveal.text: Module imports form directed edges and you need to detect A→B→C→A. You are learning to use DFS path state to distinguish a back edge from an edge into an already finished branch.

spans.text: Module imports form directed edges and you need to detect A→B→C→A.
You are learning to use DFS path state to distinguish a back edge from an edge into an already finished branch

reveal.text: Treating every edge to any previously visited module as a cycle creates false positives.

spans.text: finished nodes and ancestors on the current path are conflated

reveal.text: Track active/on-path state separately from finished state. Reaching an active ancestor closes a directed cycle.

spans.text: DFS active path versus fully finished vertices

reveal.text: Directed DFS cycle detection. Trigger: directed dependencies where cycles matter

spans.text: Directed DFS cycle detection
directed dependencies where cycles matter

reveal.text: Build graphs, import graphs, task dependencies, and workflow prerequisites use the same active-path reasoning.

modules.title: Handle dependencies and connectivity without repeated traversal

nodes.title: Dependency order exists only if the prerequisites do not chase each other in a circle

reveal.text: Database migration must finish before API deploy; API deploy before smoke tests. You are learning to produce a prerequisite-respecting order and recognize when a cycle makes that impossible.

spans.text: Database migration must finish before API deploy; API deploy before smoke tests.

reveal.text: A generic sort by task name or priority can put dependents before prerequisites.

reveal.text: Build a DAG and topologically order it. If a directed cycle exists, no complete prerequisite-respecting order can exist.

spans.text: directed prerequisites and remaining dependency counts / DFS finishing structure

reveal.text: Topological ordering. Trigger: must happen before dependencies in a directed acyclic graph

reveal.text: Builds, deployments, course prerequisites, and workflow stages use the same dependency-order structure.

nodes.title: If links only get added and you keep asking 'same component?', stop re-traversing the graph

reveal.text: Network links come online over time and the system repeatedly asks whether two devices are connected somehow. You are learning to recognize dynamic connectivity under edge additions as a union/find problem.

spans.text: Network links come online over time and the system repeatedly asks whether two devices are connected somehow.

reveal.text: Running a fresh BFS after every link/query repeats large traversals even though the only output is same-component membership.

spans.text: path structure is recomputed when only component identity is needed

reveal.text: Union the components of each newly connected endpoint. `find(x) == find(y)` answers connectivity.

spans.text: a representative for each connected component

reveal.text: Disjoint-set union / union-find. Trigger: repeated union operations + same-component queries; actual path not required

reveal.text: Account-group merges, network components, clustering edges, and offline connectivity queries share this structure.

spans.text: maintain component identity instead of rediscovering paths

reveal.text: Can union-find directly return the shortest path between two connected devices? Answer: No — it tracks component membership, not path structure.

nodes.title: The same graph can need four completely different algorithms

reveal.text: One service graph may ask: can A reach B, fewest hops, deployment order, or minimum total latency. You are learning to choose the graph algorithm from the query and edge semantics rather than from the word 'graph'.

spans.text: One service graph may ask: can A reach B, fewest hops, deployment order, or minimum total latency.
You are learning to choose the graph algorithm from the query and edge semantics rather than from the word 'graph'

reveal.text: 'Use BFS for graphs' is as unhelpful as 'use a loop for arrays.' Different outputs require different maintained state.

spans.text: one data model is confused with one algorithm

reveal.text: Reachability → BFS/DFS. Fewest equal-cost hops → BFS. Dependency order → topo. Repeated connectivity under added edges → union-find. Nonnegative weighted shortest path → Dijkstra.

spans.text: the exact output plus whether edges are directed/weighted/dynamic

modules.title: Use weighted frontier state for shortest cost

nodes.title: Weighted shortest path: always expand the cheapest known frontier first

reveal.text: Service edges carry nonnegative latency estimates. Find the route with minimum total estimated latency. You are learning to use a priority frontier when edge costs differ but remain nonnegative.

reveal.text: Maintain tentative distances. Repeatedly take the unsettled vertex with the smallest known distance and relax its outgoing edges.

nodes.title: The heap can contain old history; the distance map is the truth

reveal.text: Your Python Dijkstra implementation pushes a new heap entry every time a shorter route is found instead of decreasing a key in place. You are learning to separate stale priority-queue entries from current canonical shortest-path state.

spans.text: Your Python Dijkstra implementation pushes a new heap entry every time a shorter route is found instead of decreasing a key in place.

reveal.text: When an entry is popped, compare it with the current `dist[v]`. If it is larger, skip it as stale.
